R001.text: Fix k,A,s as declared and temporarily assume L1: s>0. Apply M001 to X=Eucl(k), σ=s and the current A. Its Borel structure is the one fixed in D001. At a finite positive radius the summand for an empty member is zero and that for a nonempty member is (diam U_i)^s; this also vanishes on a singleton because s>0. Thus the inner infimum is precisely H^s_r(A). The radius ∞ contributes no larger value than the radius 1, since every cover admissible at 1 is admissible at ∞. Hence allowing extended radii does not enlarge the supremum over finite positive radii. Finite or other countable covers can be enumerated and padded by empty members, preserving every cost. M001 therefore gives H^s(A)=Native(Eucl(k)).measure(s)(A).

The dimension in D005 is exactly the native dimension, and is nonnegative since it takes values in [0,∞]. Under s>0, s defines a nonnegative real source exponent. Apply M002 when s<dim_H(A) to obtain native measure ∞, and apply M003 when dim_H(A)<s to obtain native measure zero. In both cases F001 identifies this value with H^s(A). If H^s(A)=0, F001 makes the native measure different from ∞, so M004 gives dim_H(A)≤s. If H^s(A)=∞, F001 and M005 give s≤dim_H(A). Each conditional source use retains exactly its antecedent; no conclusion is asserted without that antecedent.

For positive δ, decreasing δ restricts the admissible covers and therefore increases their infimum. All costs are nonnegative. If H^s(A)=0, every scale infimum is zero. By the defining greatest-lower-bound property, for every positive threshold a cover has cost below it: otherwise that positive threshold would be a lower bound. If H^s(A)=∞, its defining supremum supplies a scale with content>L for every finite L>0. Replacing that scale by its minimum with δ0 preserves this strict inequality and gives a scale no larger than δ0. These are implications for arbitrary positive L,δ0,δ. Discharge L1 and universally quantify k,A,s with its positivity condition, obtaining the exported conclusion.

R002.text: H002 and M012 imply that E is bounded in the Euclidean metric bornology. In Euclidean space, a bounded set has its distances from the origin bounded by a finite constant; increasing that bound to a positive number bounds each absolute coordinate of every x∈E, because for every coordinate j<n, |x_j|≤(∑_{j<n}|x_j|^2)^(1/2). Thus there exists R>0 such that E⊆[−R,R]^n. This interpretation uses precisely the metric bornology, whose bounded sets lie in some finite-radius ball.

Choose R from F001. For arbitrary s>0,δ>0, cover E by the open balls of radius δ/2 centered at every point of Eucl(n). They cover since each point belongs to its own ball. Each ball is open in D001's metric topology, and its diameter is≤δ by the triangle inequality. H002 and M013 supply a finite subcover. Thus a finite ball-cover with these diameters exists for every positive δ.

For each positive s and δ in F002, choose its finite subcover T. Each ball's s-cost is≤δ^s, so the finite cost sum is finite. The infimum H^s_δ(E) is no greater than that cost, and is therefore finite. This proves the universally quantified finite-cover and content clauses in the exported conclusion.

First assume L1: n≥1. For 0<h≤1 partition each coordinate interval [−R,R] into at most ceil(2R/h) closed subintervals of length≤h. Their products cover the box and hence E. The number of cubes (possibly shorter at the boundary) is≤(2R/h+1)^n≤C h^(−n), where C=(2R+1)^n depends only on the fixed box. Each diameter is≤√n h by summing the squared coordinate differences. For s>n the total s-cost is≤C n^(s/2) h^(s−n), which tends to zero as h↓0 by M015 with y=s−n>0 and source variable 1/h; the factor C n^(s/2) is fixed and finite. For any fixed target scale, h can be arbitrarily small while √n h is below it; hence every scale content is zero and H^s(E)=0. N001 gives D≤s for every s>n. It follows that D≤n: if D>n, choose a finite real s strictly between n and D (also possible if D=∞), contradicting D≤s. Discharge L1. In the remaining case L2: n=0, Eucl(0) has only the empty vector; H001 implies E=Eucl(0). Its singleton cover has zero s-cost for every s>0, so N001 gives D≤s for every positive s, whence D=0. Discharge L2. Nonnegativity in both cases is N001, giving 0≤D≤n and all the remaining clauses of the exported conclusion.

R003.text: Fix B,ρ,η and assume L1: B is nonempty, ρ≥0, every pair in B has distance≤ρ, and η>0. For any b0∈B the pairwise bound puts B⊆[b0−ρ,b0+ρ]; since B is nonempty, such a center exists and proves both boundedness conditions. M016 and M017 therefore give a real least upper bound and a real greatest lower bound of B. Each is unique by order antisymmetry; denote them sup B and inf B. For every b'∈B, all b∈B satisfy b≤b'+ρ; the least-upper-bound property gives sup B≤b'+ρ. Thus sup B−ρ is a lower bound for B, so the greatest-lower-bound property gives sup B−ρ≤inf B. Therefore sup B−inf B≤ρ, including ρ=0.

Define J=(inf B−η/2,sup B+η/2) using the endpoints established in F001. Every element of B lies between inf B and sup B, and η>0 makes both endpoint containments strict. The interval is nonempty, open and bounded. Its length is sup B−inf B+η≤ρ+η by F001. Discharge L1 and quantify B,ρ,η to obtain precisely the exported conclusion. This argument asserts no measurability of B.

R004.text: In the case L1: n=0, N002 gives E=Eucl(0), a singleton, and D=0. The coordinate map t↦((),t) preserves Euclidean distances by D001. For any a>1, the N equal closed pieces of I therefore give a cover of F of maximum diameter 1/N and total a-cost N(1/N)^a=N^(1−a)→0 as N→∞ by M015 with y=a−1>0 (restricting the real variable to positive integers). For any fixed scale the same covers eventually have smaller diameter, so H^a_δ(F)=0 at every δ>0 and H^a(F)=0. N001 implies dim_H(F)≤a for all a>1 and hence dim_H(F)≤1=D+1. Discharge L1; this also proves the more precise zero-measure assertion for n=0, since q>D=0 gives a=q+1>1.

Assume L2: n≥1, q>D, 0<r≤1, and ε>0. N002 gives D≥0, so q>0. N001 gives H^q(E)=0 and an r-cover U0 of q-cost<ε/2. Discard empty members. Each zero-diameter nonempty member is a singleton, since all its pairwise distances vanish. Replace its member at original index i by an open ball about that point of positive diameter≤r and q-cost<ε 2^(−i−2). Such balls exist in Eucl(n) because n≥1: a radius smaller than both r/2 and (ε 2^(−i−2))^(1/q)/2 works, and the ball has positive diameter. Leave positive-diameter members unchanged. Countable choice makes these replacements simultaneously. The added cost is bounded by ∑_{i≥0} ε 2^(−i−2)=ε/2, so the resulting cover has positive diameters≤r and cost<ε. Discharge L2 and quantify q,r,ε to establish the indicated existence statement.

Assume L3: n≥1, q>D, 0<r≤1 and ε>0, and choose U from F002. Define r_i=diam(U_i), N_i=ceil(1/r_i), and W_(i,j)=U_i×[(j−1)/N_i,j/N_i] for 1≤j≤N_i. Since 0<r_i≤1, N_i≥1, 1/N_i≤r_i and N_i≤1/r_i+1≤2/r_i. The W form a countable cover of F: first cover the E coordinate by U_i, then partition I in the corresponding i-th fiber. Two points of the same W differ by≤r_i horizontally and≤r_i vertically, so their Euclidean distance is≤√2 r_i. Therefore ∑_{i,j} diam(W_(i,j))^(q+1) ≤ ∑_i N_i(√2 r_i)^(q+1) ≤2(√2)^(q+1)∑_i r_i^q <2(√2)^(q+1)ε. Regrouping is valid for nonnegative series, defined as suprema of finite sums. Discharge L3 and quantify the parameters, yielding the product-cover estimate for every admissible q,r,ε.

Assume L4: n≥1 and q>D. For any δ>0 define r_*=min(1,δ/√2)>0 and apply F003 with its scale argument equal to r_*. For every ε>0 the resulting cover is admissible at δ and has (q+1)-cost<2(√2)^(q+1)ε. The coefficient is positive and finite, so these costs can be smaller than any positive threshold. Nonnegativity of the infimum implies H^(q+1)_δ(F)=0. Since δ was arbitrary, taking the supremum gives H^(q+1)(F)=0. N001, with positive exponent q+1, gives dim_H(F)≤q+1. Discharge L4 and quantify q to obtain this conclusion for every q>D when n≥1.

By N002, D is finite. In the n≥1 case, F004 gives dim_H(F)≤q+1 for every q>D. One such q first makes dim_H(F) finite. If dim_H(F)>D+1, a q strictly between D and dim_H(F)−1 contradicts that inequality; hence dim_H(F)≤D+1. This is the limit q↓D without assuming a measure statement at the critical exponent. The other case is F001, and n is either zero or at least one. F001 and F004 supply the more precise zero statements in their respective cases. Thus the exported conclusion follows in full.

R005.text: Fix s,δ,V and temporarily assume L1: s>0, δ>0, V covers F, and diam(V_i)≤δ for every i. Put K={i:V_i≠∅}, ρ_i=diam(V_i), and take the projections A_i and B_i as declared. The Euclidean distance formula gives dist(x,y)≤dist((x,t),(y,u)) and |t−u|≤dist((x,t),(y,u)); hence diam(A_i)≤ρ_i≤δ and the pairwise distances in the nonempty B_i are≤ρ_i. No measurability is asserted for V_i,A_i,B_i. Put c=H^s_δ(E), finite by N002. For arbitrary ε assume L2: ε>0 and set η_i=ε 2^(−i−1)/(1+ρ_i^s)>0. N003 supplies an open interval enclosing each B_i of length≤ρ_i+η_i, including when ρ_i=0. Countable choice gives a family of such intervals.

Choose the interval family from F004 and define g_i(t)=ρ_i^s 1_(J_i∩I)(t). For t∈I and x∈E, the point (x,t) lies in F and therefore in some V_i. That index belongs to K, and x∈A_i while t∈B_i⊆J_i. Thus the A_i with t∈J_i cover E, with diameters≤ρ_i≤δ. Their s-cost bounds c by its defining infimum; replacing their diameters by the upper bounds ρ_i can only increase cost. Therefore c≤∑_{i∈K}ρ_i^s 1_(J_i)(t) for t∈I. Off I the function c 1_I vanishes, so on all ℝ we have c 1_I≤∑_{i∈K}g_i. Each J_i∩I is Borel (open interval intersected with the closed interval I), and g_i is a nonnegative measurable constant indicator. Thus each is also λ-almost everywhere measurable.

Apply M011 to the pointwise inequality F002, and M006 to its nonnegative series with countable index type K⊆ℕ. Apply M007 to I and to each J_i∩I. M008 with endpoints 0,1 gives λ(I)=1, while M009 applied to the endpoints of J_i gives λ(J_i)=|J_i|≤ρ_i+η_i. Monotonicity of the measure gives λ(J_i∩I)≤λ(J_i). The exact resulting chain is c=c λ(I)=∫c 1_I dλ ≤∫∑_{i∈K}g_i dλ=∑_{i∈K}ρ_i^s λ(J_i∩I) ≤∑_{i∈K}ρ_i^(s+1)+∑_{i∈K}η_iρ_i^s ≤∑_{i∈K}ρ_i^(s+1)+ε. The last bound follows termwise from η_iρ_i^s=ε 2^(−i−1)ρ_i^s/(1+ρ_i^s)≤ε 2^(−i−1), and ∑_{i∈K}2^(−i−1)≤∑_{i≥0}2^(−i−1)=1. All series and integrals are nonnegative extended-real expressions; splitting and comparison follow from their finite partial sums, so no convergence or integrability of the right side is assumed. Discharge L2 and generalize ε, retaining the inequality for every ε>0 under L1.

If ∑_{i∈K}ρ_i^(s+1)=∞, c≤that sum is automatic. Otherwise this sum and c are finite real numbers by F001; F003 for every ε>0 then gives c≤∑_{i∈K}ρ_i^(s+1), since a strict positive difference would be contradicted by choosing a smaller ε. Empty members have zero cost, so this is the cost of the original arbitrary V. Taking the infimum over all admissible δ-covers of F gives H^s_δ(E)≤H^(s+1)_δ(F). Discharge L1 and quantify s,δ over their positive ranges. This is the exported conclusion, with no measurability premise on the covers or their projections.

R006.text: For every a>1, divide I into N closed equal pieces. Their diameters are 1/N and total a-cost is N^(1−a)→0 as N→∞ by M015 with y=a−1>0, restricted to positive integers. At every positive target scale these covers are eventually admissible and have arbitrarily small cost. Therefore H^a(I)=0 and N001 gives dim_H(I)≤a. For all a>1 this implies dim_H(I)≤1, by the same strict-between argument on real bounds (one finite upper bound also rules out infinite dimension).

For arbitrary δ>0 let U be a countable family and assume L1: it covers I and diam(U_i)≤δ. Discard empty members by using K={i:U_i≠∅} and set ρ_i=diam(U_i). For any ε>0 apply N003 to enclose each U_i, i∈K, in an open interval J_i of length≤ρ_i+ε 2^(−i−1). Its pairwise-distance hypothesis holds by the definition of diameter. These intervals cover I. M008 gives λ(I)=1, M009 gives λ(J_i)=|J_i|, and M010 together with monotonicity of λ yields 1=λ(I)≤λ(⋃_{i∈K}J_i)≤∑_{i∈K}|J_i|≤∑_{i∈K}ρ_i+ε, since the geometric weights over K sum to at most one. If ∑ρ_i is infinite it is≥1; otherwise choosing arbitrarily small ε gives ∑ρ_i≥1. The empty members contribute zero, so ∑_i diam(U_i)≥1. Discharge L1 and quantify the cover and scale.

Fix 0<s<1 and δ>0. For every 0≤ρ≤δ, ρ^s≥δ^(s−1)ρ: if ρ=0 both sides are zero, and otherwise ρ^(s−1)≥δ^(s−1) since s−1<0. Applying this termwise to any δ-cover and using F002 gives ∑_i diam(U_i)^s≥δ^(s−1)∑_i diam(U_i)≥δ^(s−1). Taking the infimum gives H^s_δ(I)≥δ^(s−1). As δ↓0 this lower bound tends to ∞ by M014 with y=s−1<0, hence H^s(I)=∞. N001 implies dim_H(I)≥s for every 0<s<1. If dim_H(I)<1, a real s between max(0,dim_H(I)) and 1 contradicts this. Combining with F001 proves dim_H(I)=1 as well as the stated infinite-measure assertion.

Fix k,A,e and assume L2: e(I)⊆A and dist(e(t),e(u))=|t−u| for all t,u∈I. For any countable δ-cover V of A at any positive δ, put P_i={t∈I:e(t)∈V_i}. These sets cover I. By distance preservation, every pair of points in P_i has distance at most diam(V_i), so diam(P_i)≤diam(V_i)≤δ. Therefore for every s>0, H^s_δ(I)≤∑_i diam(P_i)^s≤∑_i diam(V_i)^s. Taking the infimum over V gives H^s_δ(I)≤H^s_δ(A). This proof works for every positive s,δ and does not require any cover measurable. Taking suprema gives H^s(I)≤H^s(A). For 0<s<1, F003 therefore gives H^s(A)=∞ and N001 gives dim_H(A)≥s; the strict-between argument yields dim_H(A)≥1. Discharge L2 and quantify k,A,e, proving the complete embedding clause and finishing the exported conclusion.

R007.text: Assume L1: D>0. By N002, D is finite. For every 0<s<D, N001 gives H^s(E)=∞. N005 gives H^s_δ(E)≤H^(s+1)_δ(F) for every δ>0. Taking the supremum over δ gives ∞=H^s(E)≤H^(s+1)(F), so H^(s+1)(F)=∞. Equivalently, the arbitrarily large small-scale contents provided by N001 transfer directly through N005. Applying N001 to F at exponent s+1>0 yields dim_H(F)≥s+1. Let s↑D: if dim_H(F)<D+1, choose 0<s<D with s>dim_H(F)−1, possible since D>0 and the strict inequality holds; this contradicts dim_H(F)≥s+1. Thus dim_H(F)≥D+1 under L1. Discharge L1.

Assume L2: D=0. H001 provides x0∈E; define e:I→Eucl(n+1) by e(t)=(x0,t). By D007 its image lies in F. By D001, dist(e(t),e(u))=sqrt(dist(x0,x0)^2+|t−u|^2)=|t−u| for all t,u∈I. Thus N006 applies with k=n+1 and A=F and gives dim_H(F)≥1. Since D=0, this is dim_H(F)≥D+1. This argument includes n=0 and requires no positive-diameter balls in Eucl(0). Discharge L2.

N002 gives D≥0, hence either D>0 or D=0. F001 and F002 yield dim_H(F)≥D+1 in all cases. N004 gives the matching upper bound. Antisymmetry implies dim_H(F)=D+1. Substituting D=dim_H(E), I=[0,1] and F=E×I under the Euclidean coordinate identification gives exactly dim_H(E×[0,1])=dim_H(E)+1 in Eucl(n+1), which is P.
